title: Midpoint Revision
oneLiner: A pause to connect everything so far: how a model is trained, built, squeezed into memory, made to generate text, served cheaply and specialised.

what.html:
This session ties together Sessions 2–7. The same few ideas keep returning: attention compares every token with every other, memory (not maths) is usually what limits us, and each technique trades something (accuracy, memory, speed or cost) for something else.

Everyday versionHalfway through building a house: the foundations (training), the frame (architecture), the wiring that keeps costs down (efficiency), the front door people actually use (serving), and the custom interior (fine-tuning). Time to walk through every room before adding the next floor.

why.html:
• Real design questions mix topics from several sessions.
  • The second half (alignment, prompting, retrieval, agents) builds on these.
  • A handful of formulas answers most numeric questions.

how.title: The whole journey
how.html: Train → build → fit in memory → generate → serve → specialise. Each step answers a problem raised by the one before.

how.title: Attention once more
how.html: Score each pair of tokens, hide the future, turn scores into weights, and mix the values. Twice the text means four times the scores.

how.title: Training and scaling
how.html: Compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. About 20 training tokens per parameter is the compute-optimal balance.

how.title: Architecture and memory
how.html: Training costs about 16 bytes per parameter; inference weights shrink with quantization; the KV cache grows with context and shrinks with shared heads.

how.title: Serving
how.html: Speed per word is set by memory reading. Smaller weights, batching and guessing ahead (speculative decoding) push speed up and cost down.

how.title: Fine-tuning and practice
how.html: SFT and LoRA specialise a model. Then six quick calculations that use everything above.

demo.html: Sort each idea into the part of the first half it belongs to.

example.html:
Attention by hand. Three tokens; the first can only see itself, so its output is just its own value (1, 2). The second splits its attention 33% / 67% between tokens 1 and 2, giving (0.33, 1.33).

Supplementary Some techniques only change speed (FlashAttention, speculative decoding, paged attention) and never the answer; others (quantization, pruning, sparse attention) can change the answer slightly.

misunderstandings: Bigger models just need more GPUs.
They also need proportionally more data.
Faster GPUs (more FLOPs) speed up chat replies.
Decode is limited by memory bandwidth.
Fine-tuning is the fix for everything.
Prompting and retrieval often come first.
takeaways: Decode is bandwidth-bound; batch, quantize, speculate.
SFT + LoRA specialise; guard against forgetting.
thirty: First-half summary. Pre-training: next-token prediction on filtered, deduplicated, BPE-tokenized text; C ≈ 6ND (70B × 1.4T ≈ 5.9×10²³); Chinchilla ≈ 20 tokens/param. Architecture: pre-norm RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, MoE (2/8 = 25% active). Attention softmax(QKᵀ/√d + causal mask)V costs n² (2000 tokens = 4× 1000). Training memory: Adam 16 B/param; mixed precision, sharding, checkpointing; FlashAttention exact and tiled; Ring Attention for long context. Serving: prefill (compute-bound) and decode (bandwidth-bound); greedy, beam, top-k, top-p (0.9 keeps 3 of 0.5/0.25/0.15/0.10), temperature; KV cache 524,288 B/token for 32 × 4096 × 16-bit; GQA/MQA/MLA; quantization (4 → 1 → 0.5 GB per 1B), speculative decoding, continuous batching, paged attention; $2/h at 100 tok/s ≈ $5.56 per million. Fine-tuning: SFT, instruction tuning, LoRA (r = 8 on 1000² = 1.6%), QLoRA, merging, distillation, forgetting.
